opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most underappreciated opportunities right now, and it's become urgent because of how fast AI itself is driving power demand.

For a long time, data centers were treated as a flat, inflexible load. You plug them in and they draw roughly the same power around the clock, and the utility has to plan around that. That made sense when the priority was uptime above everything else. But as data centers become a really meaningful share of total grid demand in certain regions, that assumption gets very expensive. Utilities either have to build a lot of new generation and transmission to cover the peak, or they tell you to wait years for an interconnection.

What's changed is that a lot of the load inside a data center is actually more flexible than people assumed. Not all compute is equally time-sensitive. A big training run or a batch inference job can often be shifted by minutes or hours, or moved to a different site, without anyone noticing. On the facility side, the cooling system has thermal inertia. You can pre-cool, ride through a short peak, and recover afterward, as long as you stay within safe operating limits. Then you have on-site batteries and backup generation that mostly sit idle.

The hard part is that coordinating all of that in real time is a really complex control problem. You're juggling grid signals, electricity prices, weather, IT workload forecasts, equipment constraints, and reliability requirements all at once, and they're all interacting. That's exactly where AI shines. When we worked on data center cooling optimization, the lesson was that these systems are too complex and too dynamic for static rules or human operators tweaking setpoints. A learning-based controller that understands the whole system can find efficiencies people simply wouldn't see.

If you extend that from inside one facility out to the grid, you get something powerful. A data center could act less like a passive consumer and more like a flexible grid asset. It can soak up power when renewables are abundant and cheap, back off during peak stress events, and give the grid operator a reliable, fast response. There's been analysis suggesting that even modest flexibility, curtailing a small percentage of load for a limited number of hours a year, could unlock a lot of new capacity on the existing grid. That could be the difference between connecting a new campus in months versus waiting years.

I want to be clear about the caveats. Operators are rightly very conservative because the cost of downtime is enormous. So any AI system doing this needs to be trustworthy, explainable, and operating inside hard safety constraints, with humans able to see what it's doing and override it. You earn that trust incrementally. You start with recommendations, then supervised control, then more autonomy once you've proven reliability.

But directionally, I'm very optimistic. There's a nice symmetry to it. AI is creating this huge new demand on the grid, and AI is also one of the best tools we have to make that demand flexible, efficient, and a good citizen of the grid rather than a burden on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses avoiding costly grid expansion and interconnection delays, but does not compare cost savings with the magnitude of energy savings or say cost savings are the greater benefit.

r002.rationale: It says workloads can shift and mentions grid signals and electricity prices, but does not propose scheduling them according to carbon-intensity signals.

r003.rationale: It says data centers are a meaningful share of grid demand and could act as flexible grid assets that back off during peak stress and provide a fast response.

r004.rationale: It mentions soaking up power when renewables are abundant, but does not explain that increasing renewable generation makes supply more stochastic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated opportunities in the whole energy transition, honestly. Let me back up a bit and explain why.

When I was at DeepMind working on the data center cooling work with Google, the thing that struck me was that a data center is one of the few really large electrical loads that is almost entirely software-controlled. Think about a steel mill or an aluminum smelter. Those are big loads too, but they have physical processes that are hard to move around. A data center is different. The compute is fungible. A training job can be paused. A batch workload can be shifted to a different hour or even a different region. The cooling system has thermal inertia you can lean on for a while. So you have this enormous, growing load that is, in principle, extremely flexible, and nobody has really taken advantage of that at scale yet.

Now, why does that matter for the grid? The grid has to balance supply and demand every second. Historically we did that almost entirely on the supply side. Demand goes up, you turn on a gas peaker. But as more of the supply becomes wind and solar, the supply side gets less controllable, and the volatility moves to places where it is harder to manage. So the question becomes, can demand start doing some of the balancing work? And data centers are the ideal candidate, because they are big, they are growing fast, and they have a brain attached to them.

The hard part is that this is a coordination problem, and I think AI is really the key to it. You have thousands of machines, workloads with different priorities and deadlines, cooling systems with physical constraints, a power contract with the utility, and a grid operator with a signal that might change every five minutes. A human operator cannot reason about all of that at once. But a learned controller can. It can forecast the load, forecast the grid condition, understand the tradeoffs between performance, cost, and carbon, and make a decision that respects all the safety constraints. That is essentially the same problem we solved for cooling, just at a bigger scale with more degrees of freedom.

And I would say the really exciting version is not just one data center responding to a price signal. It is a fleet of them, across regions, acting like a virtual power plant. If the wind is blowing in Texas and the sun is going down in California, you move the flexible work to where the clean energy is. That is a problem AI is very well suited to, and it turns what people see as a liability, AI's energy demand, into something that actually helps stabilize the grid.

I do want to be careful about one thing. Not all load is flexible. Serving a search query or an inference request to a user, you cannot delay that. So the realistic opportunity is maybe a portion of the load, not all of it. But even a portion, at the scale data centers are being built today, is gigawatts. And gigawatts of flexible, intelligent demand would be a really big deal for the grid.

r001.rationale: The response mentions performance, cost, and carbon tradeoffs, but does not say cost savings are a greater benefit than energy savings.

r002.rationale: It proposes shifting flexible batch workloads across hours or regions and moving flexible work to where clean energy is available.

r003.rationale: It describes data centers as enormous, growing flexible loads and says coordinated fleets could act like a virtual power plant, with gigawatts of demand helping stabilize the grid.

r004.rationale: It says that as wind and solar supply grows, the supply side becomes less controllable and more volatile.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a really interesting opportunity here, because a data center doesn’t just have to be a passive consumer of electricity. It can potentially be a flexible participant in the grid.

Some computing needs to happen immediately, but some can wait. If you can distinguish between those workloads, you can start asking: Could we shift this job to a time when there’s more available electricity? Could we run it in a different location? And how do we do that while still meeting our commitments to customers?

AI could help coordinate those decisions alongside cooling and other facility operations. But you have to respect the physical constraints and reliability requirements. You can’t compromise the data center’s core function to provide flexibility.

The exciting possibility is that, as these facilities grow, some of that demand could become a resource for balancing the grid. The key is making that flexibility predictable and dependable enough that grid operators can actually use it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses grid flexibility but does not compare cost savings with energy savings.

r002.rationale: It suggests shifting workloads to times with more available electricity, but does not mention carbon-intensity signals.

r003.rationale: It says flexible data-center demand could help balance the grid, but does not clearly explain that the scale of electricity demand makes coordinated loads a potential resource.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss renewable generation or stochastic electricity supply.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a really interesting opportunity here, because the grid has to balance supply and demand continuously, and data centers can potentially offer flexibility on the demand side. Some computing tasks need to happen immediately, but others can wait or potentially run in a different location. If you can coordinate those decisions with what’s happening on the grid, you can move some electricity consumption to times and places where power is more available.

AI can help connect those pieces: forecasting demand, understanding the constraints of the computing workload, and adjusting how the facility operates. But the key is that you’re optimizing within real constraints. You still have to deliver the computing service reliably, keep equipment within safe operating limits, and make sure your response actually helps the grid.

So I see the potential as moving from data centers being relatively passive electricity consumers to being more responsive participants. That takes coordination with grid operators, clear incentives, and controls you can trust. AI can be part of that coordination, but it has to work as part of the larger system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shifting electricity consumption but does not identify cost savings or compare them with energy savings.

r002.rationale: It proposes moving some computing and electricity use across times and locations, but does not mention carbon-intensity signals.

r003.rationale: It says data centers could offer demand-side flexibility to help balance the grid, but does not explain that the scale of their electricity demand makes coordinated loads a potential grid resource.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss renewable generation or the stochastic nature of electricity supply.
